summary:
NOT acceptable as it stands; two real defects must land first, both of which I reproduced myself, and both of which break an invariant the plan states in prose.

(1) flow-INT-1 (major). §15.8 states one invariant — the stored text of an entity this run is re-interpreting must never reach the agent, "otherwise the agent could … echo it, and the judge would say 'same' on a real change". The program enforces it at one of its three disclosure points. My probe, one session, one store: `mk_query_by_name_tool` answers `Cannot query "T.foo" — it is or will be your task to interpret it`, and five lines later in the same tool list `mk_desugar_and_explain_tool` answers `foo: OLD TEXT: adds one to a natural number.` — the pre-change baseline, verbatim. The key matches because a WIP theory's hash is deliberately content-independent (Isabelle_RPC/Tools/theory_hash.ML:233-247), and the scan writes nothing (§5.2), so every seed's stale record is sitting there for the whole session. Two further bypasses live inside the guarded tool: the refusal is tested on the typed NAME (semantics.py:1779) while the notation fallback (:1714) and the short-name fallback (:1797) disclose the resolved key's text with no second check. The outcome is the one D2 forbids: a changed entity judged UNCHANGED, and permanently so — `_write`'s UNCHANGED row stores the NEW digest (semantic_interpretation.py:1377), so no later scan re-lists it, and `_propagate` runs only `if minted` (:1457), so the whole downstream cone stays stale.

(2) interrupt-INT-1 (major). `_stop_if_cancelled`'s bare `raise` (semantic_interpretation.py:1528) re-raises the ORDINARY exception a driver's teardown substituted for the cancellation. Under the JUDGE's nested `_run_agent` that lands in `_judge`'s `except Exception` (:1333), which by design reads any session failure as CHANGED; `_gate` then runs to `_write` and `_propagate` with no await in between. I reran the suite's own pinned scenario (test_semantic_change_gate.py:943, which asserts "nothing written") with a judge driver whose `__aexit__` converts the cancellation: plain judge → `('old a', v=1, ia=1)`, counter 1; laundering judge → `('new a', v=2, ia=2, baseline 'new a')`, counter 2, i.e. a cancelled run wrote, minted, rewrote the baseline and raised snapshots. The one-line fix (`raise asyncio.CancelledError()`) I applied through a plugin: suite byte-identical at 399/16, and the laundering case writes nothing.

Everything else I checked holds: the §3 table and the two digest-keyed predicates, eff\* and its single implementation, the rec_cache write-back, the correction fixpoint's no-await warrant, the snapshot raise, the field-disjoint writes and the counter, the lock's ML shape and its structural unreachability off the lock, the startup check's ordering, the cost breakdown, and termination of the queue loop. Suite: 399 passed, 16 failed, exactly the documented pre-existing set.

Of the 16 findings: 2 majors to fix, 7 minors to fix (one storage tidy-up, one ML handler parity, two elegance clean-ups, three test gaps), 1 proposal for the user, and 6 rejected — four of them for re-raising settled rulings or re-proposing a shape a previous judge ordered.

rulings.title: desugar_and_explain hands the agent the stored interpretation of an entity the run is re-interpreting, bypassing §15.8's refusal
rulings.rationale: Confirmed by my own probe, not on the defenders' word. One session, one throw-away store, one record for T.foo with interpretation 'OLD TEXT: …', enrolled_names == ['T.foo']: mk_query_by_name_tool refuses ('Cannot query "T.foo" — it is or will be your task to interpret it from the source.') while mk_desugar_and_explain_tool, built five lines later at semantic_interpretation.py:1836-1838 and served in the same tools list at :1839-1840, returns 'Constants:\n  foo: OLD TEXT: adds one to a natural number.' Code: desugar.py:61-66 has no parameter that could carry the refusal; desugar.py:115-123 calls Semantic_DB.query(uk) for every constant the ML side returns; Semantic_DB.query returns rec.interpretation (semantics.py:789-812); extract_nontrivial_constants (Tools/explain_term.ML:96-113) drops only infra constants and constants declared in Main or an ancestor, so a constant of the theory under interpretation is always annotated. I killed the obvious refutation myself: the record is reachable by the same key after the edit because a WIP theory's hash is deliberately content-independent (Isabelle_RPC/Tools/theory_hash.ML:233-247), and the scan writes nothing (§5.2), so every seed's pre-change record is present for the whole session. The prompt pushes the agent straight at it: _SYSTEM_PROMPT:213-216 orders every symbol unfolded, :245-247 attaches the refusal to `query` alone, and the desugar tool's own description says '**IMPORTANT:** Call this tool when you are uncertain about a syntax/notation!'. Consequence is exactly D2's forbidden outcome and it is permanent: on UNCHANGED, _write stores the NEW digest (:1377) so no later scan re-lists the entity, and _propagate runs only `if minted` (:1457). The feature is what made this load-bearing — before §5.2 removed the scan-time mint an echoed baseline cost only English quality; now the text alone decides `minted`. Not previously ruled on (I grepped all five records). The finding's own fix is too weak, which one challenger proved and I re-read on the code: the refusal is keyed on the TYPED NAME at semantics.py:1779, so a notation glyph passes it, query_by_name_raw raises UndefinedEntity, and _try_resolve_syntax_token discloses Semantic_DB.query(uk) at :1714 with no second check; the short-name fallback at :1797 does the same. A name-keyed skip bolted onto desugar leaves both open.
rulings.fix: Make the refusal a property of the RUN, keyed on the universal key at the point of disclosure. (1) In AgentTask.__init__ (semantic_interpretation.py:482) add `self.enrolled_keys: set[bytes] = set()` beside `enrolled_names`, and in `enqueue` (:517-523) add `self.entries[idx].universal_key` — enqueue is the base-class method that already fills enrolled_names, so this is the one place both are maintained; expose one predicate `may_disclose(uk) -> bool` on the task. Keep enrolled_names: it carries the spelling the refusal message shows. (2) Hand `may_disclose` to mk_desugar_and_explain_tool as an optional parameter defaulting to 'disclose everything' (so the other caller and test_interpretation_driver.py are unaffected); in the annotation loop (desugar.py:115-123) emit `  {base}: (your own task in this run — interpret it from the source)` instead of the stored text, and do NOT add that constant to `seen_constants` (the note is not an explanation). (3) Apply the same predicate in mk_query_by_name_tool at the three disclosure points on the RESOLVED key — query_by_name_raw's returned uk (semantics.py:1785), _try_resolve_syntax_token's uk (:1714) and the short-name fallback's uk (:1797). The early name test at :1779 may stay as a cheap first cut that saves a round trip, but it is no longer the guard. (4) Let the tools say why at the point of use rather than editing _SYSTEM_PROMPT: prompt wording is step-8/§12 work. (5) Tests beside test_semantic_change_gate.py:403 (`test_the_query_tool_refuses_a_dependent_from_the_moment_it_is_enrolled`): after a CHANGED verdict enrols b, a desugar call whose constant list contains b's key must not contain b's stored text, and a query whose name does not resolve but whose resolve_notation returns b's key must be refused. Both are pure Python over the existing scripted fixtures. Re-review must check that every site that reads a stored interpretation inside an interpretation session goes through the one predicate.

rulings.title: Every blanket `except Exception` this feature wraps round connection traffic swallows IsabelleInterrupt
rulings.rationale: Nitpick: a hypothetical whose harm story is refuted by the very policy the finding invokes. The mechanical premise is true (IsabelleInterrupt ⊂ IsabelleError ⊂ Exception) and I reproduced nothing beyond it, because the claimed consequence cannot occur. I grepped every `on_interrupt =` in both repositories: 31 live declarations, every one Reraise; `Swallow` exists only in RPC.ML's datatype and its comment. So an IsabelleInterrupt reaching Python ENTAILS that ML has already re-raised out of mk_callback (RPC.ML:504-510) and call_command's finaliser has taken `else close_connection conn` (RPC.ML:935-946). rpc.py says so itself, in IsabelleInterrupt's own docstring: 'under Reraise the RPC call unwinds and the connection closes, so nothing may call back afterwards (a later callback fails with ConnectionResetError …)'. Therefore the user-facing §12 #4/#5 lines the finding dramatises cannot reach the user — `_report` (:1020-1027) goes over a socket ML has just closed and swallows the ConnectionResetError — and `run_state.prefilter_disabled` dies with the run (the RunState lives in the lock connection's on_close closure, :409-416). What is left is one misleading line in the host log of a process that is ending. Decisively, the proposed guard does not establish the property it is sold on: once the socket is closed every subsequent touch in those same handlers raises an ordinary ConnectionResetError (rpc.py:137-142) with byte-identical consequences, and `except IsabelleInterrupt: raise` does not touch that path — which is the path an interrupt almost always takes, since the ML thread sits in read_tagged for minutes while Python runs LLM turns. The residue window the finding calls new is not new: plan §8.1 'Release ordering' specifies it verbatim, on an ML interrupt, naming call_command's finaliser and rpc.py's 3 s grace, and records it as accepted. Adding four `except IsabelleInterrupt: raise` clauses would install a four-site obligation to remember while closing nothing measurable.
rulings.fix: No change. If the user ever wants the four sites to carry the idiom for consistency with semantics.py:1800/1816, it is tidiness, not a fix, and must not be described as making them interrupt-safe.

rulings.title: The raw-put grant is checked against the constant `_GATE_FIELDS`, not against the field dict `update_gate_fields` writes
rulings.rationale: The observation is a real, small duplication of the kind this review admits. semantics.py:995 checks `self._GATE_FIELDS`, a five-name tuple declared at :931-934 whose only non-test use is that line; `update_gate_fields` (:975-987) builds its own dict with the same five names three lines below; the checked set and the written set are linked by nothing but two hand-kept spellings, and the `who` string names `gate_write`, a method that writes no field at all. The tight shape exists in the same file: `backfill_field` checks `(field,)` at :1042, the very field it passes to `_put_fields` at :1057. I confirmed the escape is narrow, not wide: `_put_fields` does `_decode(raw)._replace(**fields)` / `Record(**fields)` (:832-836), so an unknown NAME still raises; the only unchecked edit is adding an EXISTING embedded-document field to the five keyword-only parameters. So no failure is reachable today, and the severity is minor at most. Two things in the finding are wrong and must not be carried into the fix. Its motivation misreads §10: the `from_collection` / `name` case at plan:746 is about `put_interpretation`, which calls invalidate_vectors first (semantics.py:966) and needs no grant — the catalogue case points away from widening update_gate_fields. And its proposed fix is concretely broken: moving the check into `_put_fields` puts backfill_field's currently-once, before-any-transaction check (:1042) inside the per-key loop, so `backfill_field("interpretation", [])` would raise nothing — which is exactly what test_semantic_change_gate_storage.py:228-233 asserts twice, deliberately with an empty list. It would also re-open the data-dependent invalidate/check dispatch an earlier review round explicitly forbade.
rulings.fix: Three lines, entirely inside Gate_Writer; do NOT touch `_put_fields`. In `update_gate_fields` (semantics.py:984-987) bind the dict first and check the dict it actually writes: `fields = dict(semantic_digest=…, deps=…, version=…, interpreted_at=…, baseline_interpretation=…)` / `self._db._check_raw_put_grant("update_gate_fields", fields)` / `return self._db._put_fields(self._txn, key, fields)` — `_check_raw_put_grant` is already typed `Iterable[str]` and a dict iterates its keys. Then delete `_GATE_FIELDS` with its comment (:931-934) and the check at :995. Retarget test_semantic_change_gate_storage.py:213-224 to widen the WRITTEN dict rather than the tuple — two direct calls on the helper, mirroring `test_backfill_field_keeps_its_grant_check` two tests below, keeping the pytest.raises messages with the new `update_gate_fields(…)` prefix. `test_backfill_field_keeps_its_grant_check` (:228-233) stays untouched and still passes. Plan §6.4's sentence ('The gate-field names are asserted disjoint from `_EMBEDDED_DOC_FIELDS`') stays true as written: the dict's keys ARE the gate-field names. No plan edit.

rulings.title: PROPOSAL: `update_gate_fields` is a five-field overwrite although its only caller changes one field and copies the other four back verbatim
rulings.rationale: Correctly filed as a proposal: §6.4 (plan:570-572) and §15.7 (plan:1372-1379) fix the five-field signature, so narrowing it relaxes the plan and is the user's call. The factual core is exactly true — `grep -rn update_gate_fields` finds one production caller, semantic_interpretation.py:1413, which reads `r = task.rec_cache[…]` at :1408 and passes `semantic_digest`, `deps`, `version`, `baseline_interpretation` straight back, changing only `interpreted_at`; and a challenger measured that replacing the writer with a one-field put leaves the gate suite at 37 passed, identical to baseline, with legacy-arity padding preserved. Two of the finding's three arguments are refuted and must be dropped before this goes to the user. The safety argument ('a writer that takes only what it changes cannot rewrite a committed version') fails: `ia` is itself computed from the same `r` at :1410 (`_EffStar(task.rec_cache).eff_value(r.version or 0, r.deps)`), so a wrong `r` still writes a wrong snapshot, and `_write`:1363-1364 and :1376-1377 keep the identical copy-back on the wider path anyway. The 'makes the grant check exact' argument fails: `_GATE_FIELDS` already equals the five keys character for character, and after storage-S2's fix the check reads the written dict regardless. So the real gain is smaller and cleaner than claimed: four inert round-trip arguments removed, and the operation finally carries the plan's own name for it — §5.3.1 calls it 'the snapshot raise' and the code's own failure note at :1411 already says 'while raising the interpreted_at snapshot of'.
rulings.fix: Put it to the user as a naming/tidiness question, not a safety fix. If accepted: `Gate_Writer.raise_snapshot(key, *, interpreted_at) -> Record` delegating to `_put_fields(self._txn, key, {"interpreted_at": interpreted_at})` with no `create=True` (so a missing key still raises LookupError and test_semantic_change_gate_storage.py:194-201 keeps its meaning); semantic_interpretation.py:1413-1416 collapses to one line, with :1408-1410 (`r`, the assert, the eff*) unchanged. Tests: move the version/baseline assertions of :145-155 onto `put_interpretation`; keep the legacy-arity parametrisation on the new writer (it still inherits position/from_collection from the stored record, which is why the step-3 re-review parked it there) and drop only its `(version, baseline) == (8, 'b')` line; rename the five call sites. Plan edits by hand at §6.4:570-572, §15.7:1372-1379, §10:748-749. Costs to state honestly: five test call sites, three plan edits, and the loss of the symmetry in which both gate writers name the whole gate tuple the verdict decided. If the user declines, nothing is owed — the code is the plan's shape and defect-free on this point.

rulings.title: A gate cancelled during its judge session swallows the cancellation and still writes and mints
rulings.rationale: Reproduced independently, with my own probe built from the suite's own harness, and the fix measured. Mechanism, traced on the code: `_stop_if_cancelled` ends in a bare `raise` (semantic_interpretation.py:1528) which re-raises the ORDINARY exception the arm is handling; when that arm is the judge's nested `_run_agent` (called at :1332) the exception lands in `_judge`'s `except Exception` (:1333), whose whole job is to turn any session failure into CHANGED; `_gate` then runs from :1449 through `_write` (:1455) and `_propagate` (:1457) with no await in between, so the cancellation can never be delivered again. My probe runs the suite's own pinned scenario (test_semantic_change_gate.py:943, which asserts `_rec("a").interpretation == "the a", "nothing written"`) twice, differing only in the judge driver's teardown: plain judge → outcome CancelledError, record ('old a', v=1, ia=1, baseline 'old a'), counter 1. Laundering judge (`__aexit__` raising RuntimeError('cost flush failed during teardown') on a CancelledError — byte for byte the shape the suite already models at test_interpretation_driver.py:409-418) → outcome CancelledError, record ('new a', v=2, ia=2, baseline 'new a'), counter 2, with the log line 'judge: the session on constant T.a failed; verdict CHANGED'. A cancelled gate wrote, minted, replaced the baseline, raised the snapshot and advanced the counter. The trigger is production: rpc.py:366-369 cancels the handler 3 s after the socket closes, and the judge session is built by the same factory and the same real driver class as the interpretation session (:1791-1799), whose teardown delegates into the SDK client's subprocess teardown (claude_code.py:494-497) and, for Codex, into an unguarded unregister_session (codex.py:276-279). This contradicts the plan twice — §5.4 'except Exception only, so a cancellation propagates' (plan:382) and `_judge`'s own docstring at :1327 — and it defeats the helper introduced for exactly this laundering. The one honest mitigation is direction: the escaping verdict is CHANGED, the conservative side, so the cost is a spurious mint plus a needlessly invalidated cone, never a stale entity believed fresh. I still rate it major: it is a durable, permanent write on a run that is being torn down, against an invariant the suite states and the plan states twice, and it reaches production through the ordinary user interrupt. I measured the fix: with `raise asyncio.CancelledError()` at :1528 the whole suite is byte-identical to baseline (399 passed, 16 pre-existing failures), test_interpretation_driver.py's teardown test still ends as the gate's OSError with gates_running == 0, and my probe's laundering case writes nothing (record unchanged, counter 1).
rulings.fix: (1) semantic_interpretation.py:1528: `raise asyncio.CancelledError()` instead of the bare `raise`. Raised from inside the arm's `except`, the laundered exception is kept as `__context__`, so nothing is lost from the traceback; no `except Exception` anywhere can then re-swallow it, and the helper also becomes correct when called outside an `except` arm (a bare `raise` there is a RuntimeError). (2) Log the laundered exception in the helper before raising (`_log.info("agent: the session is being cancelled; its teardown raised instead of the cancellation", exc_info=True)`): the helper is the FIRST statement of every arm (:1566, :1571, :1581, :1604), before that arm's own logging, so after the change it would otherwise be logged nowhere. (3) Rewrite the docstring sentence at :1523-1525 ('A bare `raise` re-raises the exception the calling arm is handling') to say it raises a cancellation with the arm's exception as context, and why: `_judge`'s `except Exception` would otherwise read it as a failed session, answer CHANGED, and let the gate write and mint on a run being torn down. (4) Pin it beside test_semantic_change_gate.py:943: the same scenario with a `_ScriptedJudge` subclass whose `__aexit__` converts the cancellation, asserting the record unchanged AND the counter unmoved (the counter assertion is what catches a mint a text-only assertion would miss). Do NOT take the local alternative of calling `_stop_if_cancelled()` at the head of `_judge`'s handler: it fixes one site and leaves the trap armed for the next `except Exception` placed above a nested `_run_agent`. Plan edits at §15.1's table row and §15.4 (listed separately).

rulings.title: The lock acquire raises `Remote_Calling_Failure` uncaught, so its failure reaches the user as a raw ML exception value
rulings.rationale: The bare fact is true and it is this feature's own code: Tools/semantic_store.ML:2297 calls `Remote_Procedure_Calling.call_command' try_acquire_cmd c ()` with no handler, while `check_embedding_service` — added by the same feature, three declarations below at :2314-2321 — converts `Remote_Calling_Failure` through `interpretation_rpc_error`, as do `send_for_interpretation` (:1878) and `dry_run_payload` (:1906). The gap is one notch wider than the finding says: the siblings go through `call_command`, which does `get_connection` INSIDE the caller's handler (RPC.ML:935-936), whereas :2294 hoists the connect out, so the connection-layer failure escapes raw here too. A reachable trigger exists and is specific to this call: `try_acquire_interpretation_lock` is the feature's new procedure name, and an older Python half answers `Unknown procedure …` (rpc.py:350), which RPC.ML:572 turns into `Remote_Calling_Failure`; the step-7 commit message records exactly that skew having existed in this repository. Three of the finding's supporting claims are false and must not survive into the write-up. 'Truncated at ML_print_depth': I checked the ML system this distribution pins (etc/components:44 → polyml-5.9.2-2) and its string pretty printer ignores the depth argument outright (src/basis/String.590.sml:1087-1088, `fun print_string _ _ (s: string) = PolyML.PrettyString(concat[…])`), so nothing is clipped — the real loss is cosmetic, an ML record dump with the message escaped onto one line instead of the pipeline's error line. 'The FIRST Python contact of every live run, and for Semantic_Store.collect the only one that can speak': false on both paths — semantic_interpretation_app.ML:94-96 (`resolve_roots`) runs `Theory_Hash.store_theory_hash` and `Remote_Procedure_Calling.load` first, and interpret_command.ML:89-99 runs those plus the whole dry run. 'extract_user_error's marker unwrapping is bypassed': inert, since `_try_acquire_interpretation_lock` (semantic_interpretation.py:390-417) can mint no USER_ERROR_MARKER, so the handler always takes the NONE branch. And the title's 'the one interpretation RPC with no handler' is wrong: seven other `call_command` sites in the same file lack one (:343, :361, :368, :383, :810, :2132, :2520, :2565), two of them (`is_interpreted`, `mark_interpreted`) running inside the very lock. So: a genuine small consistency defect in code this feature added, message quality only — minor, not major.
rulings.fix: Give the acquire the conversion its sibling has, inside the `\<^try>` body so the finaliser still closes the connection: `if (Remote_Procedure_Calling.call_command' try_acquire_cmd c () handle Remote_Procedure_Calling.Remote_Calling_Failure {message, ...} => interpretation_rpc_error message) then SOME (body ()) else NONE`. `interpretation_rpc_error` is in scope (defined :1458) and raises `error`, which still runs the finaliser, so the connection is closed and the lock released. Optionally, for full parity with the siblings, bring the hoisted `get_connection` under the same handler so RPC.ML:674's 'attached RPC host busy/stalled' converts too — that is a small restructure of :2288-2299 and is the implementer's call. Do NOT take the wider variant of hanging ONE handler on `interpret_with_parallel` and deleting the inner ones: it relabels in-run `is_interpreted` / `mark_interpreted` failures as 'Semantic interpretation RPC failed: …', a behaviour change beyond this finding that is the user's to accept. Plan edit at §8.2's illustrative block (listed separately).

rulings.title: The run's work set is computed by two separate expressions — `plan_interpretation` and an inline copy
rulings.rationale: Rejected on three independent grounds; the central contrast is factually wrong. (1) The inline expression is NOT 'what actually runs'. `work` (Tools/semantic_store.ML:2349) is used at exactly two places — `n_units = length work + length proofs` (:2353) and the `if null work` short-circuit (:2376). What is handed to the scheduler is `cone`, the whole cone (:2377 `interpret_cone driver config_cb force cone`), and what decides per node whether a theory is interpreted is a THIRD application of the same predicate inside the task body, `if skip_interpreted force thy then …` (:2038), which must re-evaluate at task-execution time because an already-interpreted node is still scheduled as a relay task (:2033-2035). So sharing `plan_interpretation` would not even protect the live run. (2) The 'step 6 raised the stakes' escalation is empty: `n_units` includes `length proofs`, which `plan_interpretation : bool -> theory list -> theory list` structurally cannot report, and §5.6 (plan:500-503) orders the startup check to reuse 'the opening block's own `n_units = 0` guard' — a number derived from the LIVE run's units, which is the correct input and never reads the quote. (3) It re-raises a shape the user approved item by item: CHECK_OUTDATE_PLAN.md §8, '2026-07-27 逐项批准', specifies level 1 as `filter_out (skip_interpreted force) (collect_cone roots)` and says of the function 'the body is demoted to a private function (keeping the NAME, so that semantic_store.ML's "quote set = actual work set, equal by construction" comment can lean on it)'. The code implements that to the letter. The proposed fix is also unusable in both branches: the writeln at :2203-2208 announces the sequential one-RPC-per-theory pass it precedes (its own comment says so at :2204), so it cannot move to the caller, which regains control only after that pass; and 'becomes a flag' adds a boolean printing parameter to a four-line function, which on the live path would print a new user-visible line — §12 wording, the user's call. What is genuinely duplicated is one composition of two already-shared named functions, `collect_cone` (:1936) and `skip_interpreted` (:1950), where any real future filter belongs and reaches all three sites automatically.

rulings.title: Two ways to reach the run's state: `task.run_state` and `current_run_state()`, and the startup check WRITES through the second
rulings.rationale: Rejected: the headline is false and the proposed fix is a measured regression. There are not two ways to reach the state. `current_run_state()` has exactly two call sites in the package (grep: semantic_interpretation.py:1664 and :2004); `task.run_state` is not a second accessor, it is the value the single accessor returned at :1664 and threaded at :1811 — which is literally what §15.8 mandates ('interpret_file resolves it ONCE at its top and hands it to the task'). The cross-language dependency the finding calls an accident is enforced structurally and pinned: `check_embedding_service` is absent from the SEMANTIC_STORE signature, its sole call site (:2372) is inside `interpret_with_parallel'`, which is inside `local` (:2333) … `in` (:2396) … `end` (:2403) whose only export is `interpret_with_parallel = with_interpretation_lock (…)` (:2400-2401), with the comment at :2398-2399 saying exactly that; and archive/tests/test_interpretation_lock.py:81-103 is a test named for this very property ('the check writes current_run_state().prefilter_disabled; with the lock held that is the run's own state, not a dropped fresh one'). That is the shape this review's own criterion prefers. The fix is worse than the code on both halves: `claim_prefilter_disable()` exists for a race between concurrent gates inside one failing embed call (its docstring, :368-371), which a once-per-run check running before any theory starts cannot have, so the branch's false arm is unreachable — and it would couple §12 #4 to the token that owns §12 #5, two different diagnoses. And `current_run_state() -> RunState | None` was measured to raise AttributeError in `_check_embedding_service`, which semantic_store.ML:2320-2321 turns into a fatal `error` on the user's command, while forcing `current_run_state() or RunState()` into the two existing off-lock test fixtures — spelling the throwaway twice to abolish it once. The one residue (an attribute assigned from outside RunState at :2004) has no failure behind it.

rulings.title: `InterpretationTask.format_entries` re-forms the agent's addressing label by hand
rulings.rationale: A real, one-line duplication of the sort this review admits, and I verified the replacement is output-identical rather than taking it on trust. semantic_interpretation.py:768-769 spells `_KIND_PROMPT_LABELS.get(e.kind, "unknown")` + `f"{label} {e.name}"`, character for character what `_label` does at :275, and :770-771 appends `f": {e.prop_str}"`, character for character what `_pretty_print_entry` does at :280-281 — while the file's other three label-forming sites call the authority (`_label_to_idx` at :469, `JudgeTask.format_entries` at :839, `build_prompt` at :842). My probe over 96 entry shapes (every kind in `_KIND_PROMPT_LABELS` plus an unknown kind, empty and non-empty prop_str, four position shapes): the shipped line, the `_label`-based line and the `_pretty_print_entry`-based line agree in every case, 0 mismatches. Two claims in the finding must be struck. The title misquotes the docstring: :270-274 says the label 'must be IDENTICAL everywhere it is formed — the prompt the agent reads (`format_entries` / `_pretty_print_entry`) and the answer-routing map', i.e. it ENUMERATES format_entries as a forming site; there is no 'exactly one place' rule to violate. And the attribution to step 3 is wrong — the inline spelling predates the feature by months; step 3 only added the abstract declaration and the judge's (correct) override. What makes the change worth a diff is that the same file carries a fourth hand-copy of the same strings, the `type` enum literal at :879-883, guarded only by the NB at :117-120 warning that 'any drift silently drops every answer for that kind ("Unknown entry")' and NOT covered by the module-load asserts at :146-153. I measured that literal to equal `list(_KIND_PROMPT_LABELS.values())` exactly, order included. Doing the finding's half alone leaves the more dangerous copy standing.
rulings.fix: Two edits, one commit, both verified no-ops at HEAD. (1) semantic_interpretation.py:768-771 → `line = (f"  [line {e.line_number}] " if e.line_number > 0 else "  ") + _label(e)` followed by the existing `if e.prop_str: line += f": {e.prop_str}"`, deleting the `label = …` assignment. Route through `_label`, not `_pretty_print_entry`: the latter's only consumer, `InterpretationResult.pretty_prints`, is discarded by ML (`val (_, _, current, cumulative)`, Tools/semantic_store.ML:1876-1878), so hanging the live prompt on it would couple it to a vestigial wire field. (2) semantic_interpretation.py:879-883 → `"enum": list(_KIND_PROMPT_LABELS.values()),`, which discharges the NB at :117-120 by construction and lets that comment shrink to a pointer at `_label`. Do not bill this as a feature defect; it is a pre-existing cleanup the integration made visible, and it can ride the step-8 pass.

rulings.title: The task is used as a context manager that does nothing, and the all-cached branch builds an entry-less task to read one stored tuple
rulings.rationale: Every factual claim checks out and this is a deferred item, not a new one. `AgentTask.__enter__`/`__exit__` (semantic_interpretation.py:509-513) are `return self` / `pass`, and they are the only `__enter__`/`__exit__` in the package; nothing in either `__init__` allocates a resource, and `__exit__` returns None so it does not even suppress — `with … as task:` at :1806 and :1909 is exactly plain assignment. `git show 794de71` shows the protocol once opened and closed a RocksDB handle, so it is a vestige of a store the task no longer owns; `Self` is imported at :21 for that one dead annotation and nothing else. The all-cached branch (:1907-1913) builds `InterpretationTask(…, entries=[], …)` solely to reach `CostSummary(*task.historical_cost())`, and `historical_cost` (:605-612) touches nothing but `self.theory_key` — a function in disguise whose only production caller has to invent a receiver (test_layered_db.py:414 already routes around the constructor with `object.__new__` for the same reason). Decisively, the step-4 judge saw this shape, had to write an explicit TRAP warning about it while fixing a CONFIRMED MAJOR bug it caused ('do NOT patch the `else` branch with a `task.state`-derived list — in that branch `task` has entries=[] and state=[], so the list is silently empty and the bug survives'), and closed with 'Optional, larger, and worth raising separately rather than folding in: the `if seeds: / else:` split exists only because the all-cached branch needs an InterpretationTask to reach historical_cost() … That is a step-4 restructure, not part of this fix.' Collecting a deferred item is not re-raising a ruling. Two things to correct in the write-up: the parenthetical inventory ('label map, queue, event, ten cost accumulators, two index-aligned lists') overstates — with entries=[] every one of those is empty and the construction is microseconds, so the objection is that a fake object stands in for a one-field read, not that it is slow; and the protocol had already been dead for months before step 3 moved it.
rulings.fix: (1) Delete `__enter__`/`__exit__` (:509-513) and drop `Self` from the import at :21 (it becomes unused). (2) At :1806 use plain assignment and dedent the block; behaviour is provably identical since `__exit__` returns None. (3) Make the cost read receiver-free but keep it on `AgentTask` beside its sibling `write_cost`: either a `@staticmethod historical_cost(theory_key)` or a module helper with `historical_cost` left as a one-line delegate — the delegate form means test_layered_db.py:423 needs no edit. The all-cached branch then becomes `cumulative_cost = CostSummary(*AgentTask.historical_cost(theory_key))`, with no object in sight. (4) Do NOT take the larger variant of building the full task unconditionally: `unicode_file_path = mk_unicode_file(file_path)` (:1774) sits inside `if seeds:` and writes a Unicode copy of the theory file, so hoisting the task above it would force that I/O on every all-cached theory — the common case under `collect --reinterpret`. Sequencing: step 2 dedents ~100 lines of the hottest function for no behavioural gain, so fold this into the step-8 pass rather than spending a standalone churn commit, and verify against the documented baseline (399 passed / 16 pre-existing failures).

rulings.title: The live statement refresh runs over the scan's pre-run `not_enrolled` snapshot instead of the entity states
rulings.rationale: Rejected: it re-raises a settled ruling and its fix is the bug that ruling fixed. The step-4 judge confirmed soundness-S1 as MAJOR — 'A live run over a theory with no seeds never refreshes the statement' — precisely because the live refresh was then computed from `task.state` inside the `if seeds:` branch; its corrected_fix prescribed 'ONE unconditional call immediately before the single return', with the comment 'the scan's not-enrolled list refreshes exactly the entries this run did not write'. semantic_interpretation.py:1915-1919 IS that fix and that comment. Applying this finding's fix ('compute the set from the task inside the `with` block') would put the refresh back inside the seeded branch; and in the other live branch the task is built with `entries=[]` (:1909-1912), so `self.state = [_NOT_ENROLLED] * len(entries)` (:478) is `[]` and the proposed comprehension yields no indices at all — the all-cached theory would silently stop being refreshed, which is exactly the bug, and which archive/tests/test_semantic_change_gate_storage.py:488 (`test_a_live_run_with_no_seed_still_refreshes_the_statement`) pins. The 'remembered invariant' charge is also backwards: `_refresh_statements` re-reads `rec_cache[uk]` and compares `rec.expr != e.prop_str` (:1248-1250), i.e. it VERIFIES the property over the wider set instead of assuming it; the narrowed set would skip exactly the entries the run wrote and would silently leave a stale expr if `_write` ever changed. And the wider set is required, not merely admissible: `rec_cache` holds None for entries with no record (:1676-1677) and the refresh asserts `rec is not None` (:1249), so only the scan's 'cached and not stale' set is safe — which is what §15.8 item 6 says. The four comment lines at :1915-1918 are the surviving record of that bug and are load-bearing.
rulings.fix: No change. If the comment is ever touched, make the warning explicit rather than removing it (a `task.state`-derived list is empty in the all-cached branch).

rulings.title: The enrolled-names list crosses the seam as `working_names`, lives on the base class, and is read two ways
rulings.rationale: Rejected on all three parts, and part (b) would crash the judge. (b) 'Move the field to InterpretationTask, where the plan puts it' is not a refactor: `enqueue` is a BASE-class method and it is `enqueue` that appends the name (semantic_interpretation.py:517-523, `self.enrolled_names.append(self.entries[idx].name)`), while `JudgeTask.__init__` calls `self.enqueue(0)` at :836 and defines no `enqueue` of its own — with the field declared only on the subclass, every judge session raises AttributeError. The field must live where the method that writes it lives; the plan's §15.3 listing (plan:1041) is the loose half here, not the code, and the step-5 judge already ruled on this exact point ('#11 (`enqueue(0)` in the JudgeTask constructor) only touches the judge's own `enrolled_names` … neither of which any judge consumer reads'), so this also re-raises a settled ruling. (c) is a hypothetical with no failure, over code this feature did not write: the truthiness reads (semantics.py:1551, :1742) were introduced whole by a pre-feature commit to distinguish an interpretation session from a bare proof-assistant query session, `enrolled_names` is only ever appended to (so its truthiness is monotone), and the sole production call site sits after the enqueue loop inside `if seeds:` (:1769, :1816, :1832). Its fix — an explicit `interpretation_session=True` — replaces one source of truth with two that can silently disagree, which is the elegance criterion argued backwards. (a) is a bare rename remark about the pre-existing parameter of a function exported as public API (`__init__.py:19`, `mk_query_by_name_tool as query_by_name_tool`) that also serves non-interpretation callers; the plan asks only that the caller pass `task.enrolled_names`, and §0's glossary — the authority under the terminology rule — has no term for this list at all.
rulings.fix: No change. (Note for the flow-INT-1 fix: the enrolled KEYS belong in the same base-class place as `enrolled_names`, filled by the same `enqueue`, for the very reason that refutes part (b).)

rulings.title: The statement refresh's empty-prop_str guard is unpinned: deleting one `and` blanks stored `expr`, suite stays green
rulings.rationale: The coverage gap is real and measured (the mutation survives not just the named subset but the whole suite), and the guard is one the plan spells out verbatim with its reason (§15.8 item 8, plan:1432-1435, mirrored in the docstring at semantic_interpretation.py:1241-1245). This series has already ruled the genre fix-worthy twice (review_step5 agreement-F1, review_step7 py-S7-PY-1), and the scope puts the tests under review. But almost everything ELSE in the finding is wrong and must not reach the fix. Severity 'major' is unwarranted: there is no defect, the code matches the plan character for character, and `git log -S` puts the guard in a pre-feature commit (2026-05-22) together with the `""` it guards against. The claim that the guard 'is the only thing standing between a wire prop_str of "" and a blanked expr + a tombstoned vector' is false: `_write` passes `expr=e.prop_str` with NO truthiness test at :1385, for every ENROLLED entry, so the program does not hold that invariant at all — a test asserting it would teach a false rule. And the reachability story is refuted on the ML side: `PIDE_State.command_at_position` does not answer NONE off PIDE — it falls back to `command_at_position_wip` (Tools/pide_state.ML:631, :584-586), which re-cuts the command spans from the .thy on disk, so the headline scenario ('a locale interpreted under jEdit, re-scanned under collect') does not arise. What remains reachable is narrow: a non-.thy position (a Method registered in an ML_file), an unreadable or unparsable file (`command_spans_of_file` warns and returns []), or a constant whose constraint lookup raises (Tools/semantic_store.ML:722-723 → ""). Narrow but real, and on the dry path the guard is the difference between 'unknown statement' and 'blank the stored one plus kill its vector'.
rulings.fix: Two lines, no new fixture, and scope the assertion honestly to the path where the rule actually holds. In archive/tests/test_incremental_criteria.py beside `test_a_dry_run_refreshes_a_changed_statement_and_nothing_else` (:146), add a cached, fresh entry whose stored `expr` is non-empty and whose wire `prop_str` is "", and assert after the dry run that the raw record is byte-identical and `contains([uk]) == [True]`, with a docstring saying what it pins: an empty wire statement means 'unknown', not 'empty', so the dry path never blanks an `expr` it has no replacement for. Do NOT write a test that claims the rule holds run-wide (the enrolled path at :1385 contradicts it), and do NOT amend plan §10: §5.3.2 and §15.8 item 8 already state the requirement, and a third copy in the test list splits one rule across two sections.

rulings.title: `next_batch`'s `_QUEUED` guard is unpinned; without it an entry answered before it is sent stalls the retry loop to its give-up
rulings.rationale: This is the strongest of the three test findings and squarely within the precedent this series set (review_step5 ruled the answer tool's `_NOT_ENROLLED` refusal, an exactly analogous unpinned guard in the same tool family, a MAJOR fix). The guard at semantic_interpretation.py:532 (`if self.state[i] == _QUEUED:  # else answered ahead of its turn`) is load-bearing and reachable on an ordinary path, not only through the race the finding names: `interpret_file` enqueues the WHOLE seed set before the first turn (:1816-1817) while `_BATCH_SIZE = 20` (:155), so on any theory with more than 20 seeds most entries sit `_QUEUED` with their index in the deque, and the answer tool accepts any of them — it refuses only `_NOT_ENROLLED` (:927) — while `on_answer`'s own comment names `_QUEUED` as a source state (:737) and the tool's description invites resubmission. Nothing removes a stale index from the deque, so this guard is the only thing between it and a re-send. Both challengers reproduced the mutation surviving the entire suite (399 passed, unchanged), and one drove the real `_run_agent`/answer tool/retry loop end to end: under the mutation the entry goes `_DONE` → `_SENT` with `results[idx]` non-None (breaking the invariant stated at :352), the agent's identical re-answer is dropped by `on_answer`'s `if text == old: return` (:733), `unanswered_in_batch` keeps returning it and the run dies with `FatalAgentError … left 1 of 4 entities uninterpreted after 10 retry rounds` on an entity that was in fact written. The second branch is worse rather than absent: a re-answer differing by a byte runs a SECOND gate on a `_DONE` entity, burning a judge session against D12's cap and, on CHANGED, minting spuriously. One correction: the finding's own assertion (`assert task.next_batch() == []`) is wrong in general — with entries queued behind the answered one the batch is not empty.
rulings.fix: Add one test to archive/tests/test_interpretation_driver.py (the module whose docstring makes it the `_run_agent` harness), using its existing seams (`_make_task`, `_run`, `_answer`, the autouse gate-recording fixture) and routing the answers through the REAL answer tool, which is that module's stated policy and is half of why the guard is needed. Pin the CONSEQUENCE, not only the mechanism: a task of 4 entries with batch_size 2 whose first turn answers indices 0, 1 and the still-queued 2 must end with every entry `_DONE`, every text written once, exactly two turns (no retry round), and `T.c2` absent from the second turn's prompt. Assert at the `next_batch` level as well if desired — 'the answered index is not in the returned batch' — but not `next_batch() == []`.

rulings.title: `throttled = 0` after a completed turn is unpinned; the rate-limit backoff's jitter, cap and reset are entirely unexercised
rulings.rationale: Accepted as a test gap, with two of the finding's claims struck. What earns the fix: the jittered capped backoff with the reset is a NAMED deliverable of this feature — §13 step 3, 'the queue loop in `_run_agent` as a plain loop with the throttle arms' jitter and capped backoff (§15.4)' (plan:885) — and nothing in the suite exercises any of it. A challenger measured that not only `throttled = 0` but the whole delay expression can be replaced by `delay = 0.0` with the suite green, i.e. the 60 s cap, the doubling and the ±50 % jitter are all unpinned; and deleting the sleep turns a 429 into a tight retry loop against the provider, which nothing would notice. The one test that touches the arm (test_semantic_change_gate.py:963) disarms the observable by hand at :966 (`monkeypatch.setattr(SI.random, "uniform", lambda lo, hi: 0.0)`) and raises RateLimitError once, so the reset is unreachable in it by construction. Struck: 'the whole theory's wall clock degrades with no signal' is false — :1574 logs every wait with its length, and interpret_file:1657-1661 attaches the RPC server's handlers to this logger precisely so those lines reach the host log; and the implied accumulation across a long library run is wrong — `throttled` is a local of one `_run_agent` call, and there are two call sites (one per theory at :1865, one per judge session at :1332), so it resets at every theory and every judge boundary, exactly as the comment at :1544 says ('consecutive rate-limit hits'). The code itself is §15.4 verbatim and needs no change. Severity is minor and no higher: no verdict, no write and no record is at risk either way.
rulings.fix: One deterministic test in archive/tests/test_interpretation_driver.py, costing no wall-clock: stub `SI.random.uniform` to return 1.0 while recording its arguments (so the delay equals the base AND the ±50 % window is pinned) and capture `SI.asyncio.sleep` instead of sleeping. Script six consecutive `RateLimitError`s, then a completed turn, then one more `RateLimitError`, and assert the recorded non-zero delays are `[2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 60, 2]` — doubling, the `min(…, 60)` cap and the reset in one assertion — with `uniform` called as `(0.5, 1.5)` each time. Do NOT assert on ranges from the real `random.uniform`, and do NOT drive it through the store harness (whose runs are bounded by a 20 s `wait_for`); note also that `_run_agent`'s generic arm ends with its own `asyncio.sleep(2)` at :1612, so filter the captured values or a stray recycle wait will be read as a throttle wait.

rulings.title: §3 row 4 / §15.5 say UNCHANGED writes `rec.version`; the code writes `rec.version or w.counter_value()`
rulings.rationale: Rejected: this re-raises a ruling that is settled in writing, and the scope forbids it. The step-5 SCOPE disclosed it as implementer derivation 2, in almost the finding's own words — '`_write`'s UNCHANGED row reads a version-less record as ε (`rec.version or w.counter_value()`), the same reading as the theorem-alike row and the scan (§9 "ε epoch"); the plan's table says "unchanged". A record with a digest and a baseline but no version cannot come from the gate, but the reading costs nothing and keeps `eff_value` off a None' — and the step-5 judge ruled on it twice in verified_ok ('#2 … is unreachable in practice and keeps `eff_value` off a None'; 'Derivation 2's `rec.version or w.counter_value()` in the UNCHANGED branch is needed, not merely harmless: `_EffStar.eff_value` would raise on a None version'). Independently of the re-raise, the headline claim 'This is a real behavioural difference' is false on every reachable state: the branch requires `rec.baseline_interpretation is not None` (forced CHANGED otherwise at :1441), and a non-None baseline has exactly two writers in the package, both inside Gate_Writer, both writing it together with a version from `counter_value()` or `mint()`, which `_unpack_counter` (semantics.py:547-552) documents can never be 0 or None. So §3 row 4's 'version: unchanged' describes the shipped behaviour exactly, and §15.8 (plan:1390-1392) already states that §15.5 keeps the ε reading of a version-less record. The proposed §3 table edit would document a record shape no writer can produce.
rulings.fix: No change to semantic_interpretation.py:1376, and no edit to §3 row 4 or §15.5.

plan_edits: §15.8, the addressing-rule paragraph (plan:1440-1448). CURRENT: "the names `mk_query_by_name_tool` (:1191) refuses are `task.enrolled_names`, a list `enqueue` appends to and the tool is handed as the same mutable object (its membership test re-reads it on every call, comparing in the list's glyph spelling — `pretty_unicode(name)` — because the tool has already rewritten the agent's input to the escape form; step-4 review), so an entity enrolled by a later CHANGED verdict is refused from that moment on — otherwise the agent could be handed the stored text of the very entity it is re-interpreting, echo it, and the judge would say \"same\" on a real change." PROPOSED: state it as a property of the run rather than of one tool — "No stored interpretation of an ENROLLED entity may reach the agent: otherwise it could echo the text of the very entity it is re-interpreting and the judge would say \"same\" on a real change. `enqueue` records the entry's universal key as well as its name, and EVERY tool of the interpretation session that reads `Semantic_DB` consults that set at the point of disclosure, keyed on the universal key the lookup resolved — `mk_query_by_name_tool` (after `query_by_name_raw`, after the notation fallback and after the short-name fallback) and `mk_desugar_and_explain_tool`'s constant annotation, which answers a one-line note instead of the stored text. The names list stays for the refusal message's spelling (`pretty_unicode(name)`, step-4 review), but it is no longer the guard; a tool added later that reaches into `Semantic_DB` and does not consult the predicate re-opens the hole."

§15.1, the `_stop_if_cancelled()` table row (plan:944). CURRENT: "§15.4: called first in every recovering arm of `_run_agent`; re-raises when the current task is being cancelled". PROPOSED: "§15.4: called first in every recovering arm of `_run_agent`; raises a `CancelledError` (the arm's laundered exception kept as its context) when the current task is being cancelled, so no `except Exception` above can absorb it".

§15.4, the `_stop_if_cancelled` paragraph (plan:1121-1123). CURRENT: "the helper re-raises instead of recycling, because a recycled session would have every create_task refused and the loop would park in wait_for_progress for ever". PROPOSED: "the helper raises a `CancelledError`, not the arm's laundered exception, and logs that exception before doing so: re-raising an ordinary exception here would be swallowed again by `_judge`'s `except Exception` (§5.4 step 3) one frame above the judge's nested `_run_agent`, which reads any session failure as CHANGED and lets the gate write and mint on a run being torn down. It raises rather than recycling because a recycled session would have every create_task refused and the loop would park in wait_for_progress for ever".

§8.2, the illustrative `with_interpretation_lock` block (plan:661). CURRENT: "        if call_command' try_acquire_cmd c () then SOME (body ()) else NONE". PROPOSED: "        if (call_command' try_acquire_cmd c ()\n             handle Remote_Calling_Failure {message, ...} => interpretation_rpc_error message)\n        then SOME (body ()) else NONE", with one clause in the prose: the acquire converts an RPC-level failure exactly as `send_for_interpretation`, `dry_run_payload` and the §5.6 startup check do, so a Python half that predates the lock reaches the user as the pipeline's error line rather than as a raw `Remote_Calling_Failure` record; `error` still runs the finaliser, so the connection is closed and the lock released.

§10, the queue-loop bullet (plan:728-731). CURRENT: "- queue loop: a fake driver raising `RateLimitError` mid-turn with part of the batch answered — after the recycle every entry ends non-`None`, none interpreted twice, none lost; gates started before the recycle finish and write;". PROPOSED: append two items the suite does not pin today — "; an entry answered before its batch goes out (the whole seed set is enqueued up front while a batch is `_BATCH_SIZE`) is not re-sent by `next_batch`, so no answered entry returns to `_SENT` and the retry loop does not give up on a written entity; and the throttle arms' timing (§15.4): consecutive rate limits double and cap at 60 s with ±50 % jitter, and a completed turn resets the count — measured with `random.uniform` stubbed and `asyncio.sleep` captured, so the test costs no wall-clock".
proposals_for_user: Narrow the snapshot-raise writer (relaxes §6.4:570-572 and §15.7:1372-1379). `Gate_Writer.update_gate_fields` takes five fields; its single production caller (semantic_interpretation.py:1413) changes one and copies four back verbatim off the same record it just read. Replacing it with `raise_snapshot(key, *, interpreted_at)` over `_put_fields(txn, key, {"interpreted_at": ia})` removes four inert arguments and gives the operation the plan's own name for it — §5.3.1 calls it 'the snapshot raise' and the code's failure note at :1411 already says 'while raising the interpreted_at snapshot of'. A challenger measured the narrowed writer against the gate suite: 37 passed, identical to baseline, with legacy-arity padding and the position/from_collection inheritance preserved. Do NOT accept it on safety grounds — `interpreted_at` is itself computed from the same record at :1410, so a wrong record still writes a wrong snapshot. Price: five test call sites to move, three plan edits, and the loss of the symmetry in which both gate writers state the whole gate tuple the verdict decided. Modest gain; decline freely.

Decide once what an empty wire `prop_str` means, and enforce it at one place (relaxes §15.8 item 8's 'today's guard verbatim', plan:1432-1435). Today two writers disagree: `_refresh_statements` (semantic_interpretation.py:1250) treats "" as 'no statement text — keep what is stored', while `_write` (:1385) passes `expr=e.prop_str` with no test at all, so for an ENROLLED entry an empty wire statement blanks the stored `expr` and, through `put_interpretation`'s invalidate_vectors, kills its vector. `mk_prop_str` really does yield "" — for a non-.thy position (a Method registered in an ML_file), an unreadable or unparsable theory file, and a constant whose constraint lookup raises (Tools/semantic_store.ML:722-723). Collapsing the two onto one rule (`expr = e.prop_str or rec.expr`, or one tiny shared helper) would make the rule impossible to forget instead of asking the next reader to notice a truthiness test at one of two sites — and would make the mutation tests-F1 reports unwritable. It is a behaviour change on stored data (a re-interpreted entity whose statement could not be computed would keep its stored one), so the semantics are yours to choose: if "" is to mean 'really empty', then the refresh guard is the odd one out and should go instead.
nitpicks_rebuked: storage-S1 — hypothetical with no concrete failure, self-refuting: every live callback declares Reraise, so an IsabelleInterrupt reaching Python means the socket is already closing (rpc.py's own IsabelleInterrupt docstring says so), the §12 lines cannot reach the user, and the identical behaviour already arrives as ConnectionResetError, which the proposed guard does not touch; §8.1 already records the residue window as accepted.

ml-ML-INT-2 — misdescribes the code it indicts (`interpret_cone` is handed `cone`, and `skip_interpreted` is re-applied per node at semantic_store.ML:2038), its `n_units` escalation is empty (`n_units` includes `length proofs`, which `plan_interpretation` cannot report), it re-raises a shape the user approved item by item on 2026-07-27, and its fix is impossible in one branch and a user-visible regression in the other.

elegance-INT-1 — 'two ways to reach the run's state' is false (one accessor, two call sites, one threaded value, exactly §15.8); the cross-language dependency is enforced by `local … in … end` plus absence from the ML signature and pinned by a named test; the proposed `RunState | None` was measured to raise AttributeError and turn an off-lock no-op into a fatal error on the user's command.

elegance-INT-5 — re-raises a settled ruling and proposes the bug it fixed: the shape on disk is verbatim the step-4 judge's prescribed fix for the confirmed MAJOR soundness-S1, and a `task.state`-derived list is empty in the all-cached branch (entries=[]), which test_semantic_change_gate_storage.py:488 pins.

elegance-INT-6 — part (b) would crash every judge session (`enqueue` is the base-class method that writes the field and `JudgeTask.__init__` calls it) and re-raises a step-5 verified_ok ruling; part (c) is a hypothetical reordering over pre-existing code whose fix creates a second source of truth; part (a) is a style rename of a pre-existing public-API parameter the plan never asks to rename.

tests-F2 — re-raises a settled ruling: disclosed verbatim as step-5 implementer derivation 2 and ruled on twice in the step-5 judge's verified_ok; its 'real behavioural difference' is unreachable (a non-None baseline is only ever written together with a version ≥ 1), and its §3 edit would document a record shape no writer can produce.
